title: Choosing hyperparameters
objectives: Tune a model by cross-validation without touching the test set.

screens.title: How many neighbours
screens.prose: A $k$-nearest-neighbour model predicts a loan’s spread from the $k$ most similar loans in 300. For each $k$ from 1 to 60 the chart shows the training MSE and the 5-fold CV MSE.
screens.question: Which $k$ would you choose?

options.text: $k = 10$: the lowest CV MSE, 0.296
$k = 1$: its training MSE is 0
options.why: You chose by training error. With $k = 1$ each loan is its own nearest neighbour, so training MSE is 0. The CV MSE is the worst on the chart, 0.461.

options.text: $k = 60$: the smoothest model is the safest
options.why: Smooth is not safe here: averaging 60 loans blurs real differences, and the CV MSE climbs to 0.376.

options.text: $k = 30$: the middle of the range
options.why: The middle of the range we happened to try has no special status. Let the held-out score decide.

hints.text: Which curve uses loans the model did not see?
The solid line is cross-validated; the dashed line is scored on the fitting loans.
Read the lowest point of the solid line.

feedback.correct: The held-out curve bottoms out at $k = 10$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose by the curve that measures unseen loans.

explain.text: Training error only falls as $k$ shrinks, so it always points to $k = 1$. The CV curve falls, bottoms out at $k = 10$, then rises: too few neighbours chase noise, too many blur the signal. Choosing $k$ this way is our first tuning.

screens.title: A validation curve
screens.prose: Ridge on 200 loans with 15 features, at nine penalties $\alpha$ from 0.01 to 100. Each dot is the mean 5-fold CV MSE; each bar spans one fold sd either side. Tap the $\alpha$ with the lowest mean.
screens.question: Tap the dot with the lowest mean CV MSE.

hints.text: The dots sit almost level on the left, then rise.
Look just before the curve turns up.
The lowest dot is at $\log_{10}\alpha = 1$, that is $\alpha = 10$, with mean 0.2010.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the dot just before the curve climbs.

byKey.left: The dots on the left are 0.2025, a whisker above the dip at $\alpha = 10$.
byKey.a8: That is $\alpha = 100$, the highest mean on the chart.

explain.text: The lowest mean is 0.2010, at $\alpha = 10$. But look at the bars: every dot up to $\alpha = 30$ lies inside the others’ spread. The dip is real but small next to the fold noise.

screens.title: A grid that stops too soon
screens.prose: Ridge’s $\alpha$, like $k$, is a **hyperparameter**: set before fitting, not learned by it. Choosing it by CV is **tuning**, and the chart is a **validation curve**. A colleague tried $\alpha$ only up to 10, and the best mean sits at that edge.
screens.question: What should the colleague do?

options.text: Widen the grid past 10 until the curve turns up, then choose
Take $\alpha = 10$: it is the best tried
options.why: A best value on the edge only says the curve was still falling there. The minimum may lie beyond it.

options.text: Add more points between 0.01 and 10
options.why: Filling in the inside cannot find a minimum outside the range.

options.text: Drop the penalty: the curve is flat anyway
options.why: The flat left side says small penalties are equivalent, not that the best penalty is small.

hints.text: Where does the best dot sit in the range tried?
It is the last dot on the right.
A minimum at the edge is not yet a minimum. Try 30 and 100.

feedback.correct: A best value on the edge of a grid means widen the grid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at where the best value sits.

explain.text: Adding $\alpha = 30$ and $100$ shows the curve turning up: 0.2125, then 0.2967. Now $\alpha = 10$ is a true interior minimum. Always check that the best setting is not on the grid’s boundary.

screens.title: The one-standard-error rule
screens.prose: The dip at $\alpha = 10$ is smaller than the fold spread. The **one-standard-error rule** takes the simplest model whose mean is within one sd of the best. For ridge, simplest means most shrunk: the largest $\alpha$. Here the limit is $0.2010 + 0.0214 = 0.2224$.
screens.question: Tap the dot the one-standard-error rule picks.

hints.text: Which dots have a mean below the dashed line?
Of those, take the one furthest right.
$\alpha = 30$ has mean 0.2125, under 0.2224; $\alpha = 100$ has 0.2967, over it.

feedback.correct: $\alpha = 30$: within one sd of the best, and more shrunk.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the largest $\alpha$ whose dot sits below the line.

byKey.best: That is the best mean itself. The rule moves to a simpler model when one is within the noise.
byKey.over: At $\alpha = 100$ the mean, 0.2967, is above the line.

explain.text: Every mean below the line is within fold noise of the best, so we prefer the most shrunk, $\alpha = 30$. Textbooks often use $\text{sd}/\sqrt{k}$ as the error bar. Lesson 2 showed that understates the noise, so we use the plain fold sd.

screens.title: Two hyperparameters
screens.prose: A model can have two knobs. Here a `Pipeline` adds polynomial terms of degree 1 to 3, scales them, and fits ridge. Each cell is the 5-fold CV MSE for one pair, on 200 loans with a curved leverage effect.
screens.question: Tap the best cell.

hints.text: Look for the smallest number in the whole grid, not in one row.
Degree 2 has the lowest row.
Within degree 2 the smallest is 0.277, at $\alpha = 10$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare every cell.

byKey.deg3: That is degree 3’s best, 0.356. Degree 2 does better at 0.277.
byKey.simple: The plain linear model, 0.334, misses the curve in leverage.

explain.text: Degree 2 captures the curve; degree 3 has 119 terms and needs heavy shrinkage to survive. The best pair is degree 2, $\alpha = 10$, an interior cell on both axes. Fifteen settings times five folds is 75 fits.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_val_score

def validation_curve_ridge(X, y, alphas, k, seed):
    folds = KFold(n_splits=k, shuffle=True, random_state=seed)
    means = []
    for a in alphas:
        scores = -cross_val_score(Ridge(alpha=a), X, y, cv=folds,
                                  scoring='neg_mean_squared_error')
        means.append(round(float(scores.mean()), 4))
    return means
widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests on loans from `make_loans(n, p, seed)`, compared with math.isclose. The first run loads scikit-learn and NumPy, which takes 10 to 30 seconds; later runs are quick.
widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_loans(n, p, seed):
    """Loans: spread over base rate (percentage points). x0 leverage +0.6, x1 interest cover -0.4,
    x2 sector risk +0.3, the rest pure noise; noise sd 0.45."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, p)).round(3)
    beta = np.zeros(p)
    beta[:3] = [0.6, -0.4, 0.3][:p]
    y = (2.5 + X @ beta + rng.normal(0, 0.45, n)).round(3)
    return X, y

explain.text: One `KFold` object, reused, scores every $\alpha$ on identical folds, so the comparison is fair. Build `folds` once, outside the loop.

screens.title: The best score is not the expected score
screens.prose: You tune the 15-cell grid with `GridSearchCV`. Its `best_score_` is $-0.277$, the MSE of degree 2 with $\alpha = 10$. Your manager asks what MSE to expect on new loans.
screens.question: What is the honest answer?

options.text: 0.277, the best cross-validated score
options.why: You reported the winner’s own score. It was chosen because it was the lowest of 15 noisy numbers, so it is biased low.

options.text: Probably a little above 0.277; one score on the locked test set will say
The average of all 15 cells
options.why: That averages settings you will never use, including degree 3 at 4.653. It measures the grid, not the model.

options.text: 0.277 minus one fold sd, to allow for noise
options.why: You moved it the wrong way. Selection makes the best score optimistic, so the expected error is higher, not lower.

hints.text: Why did this cell win?
Among 15 noisy scores, the lowest has a lucky draw built in.
The winning score did the choosing, so it cannot also be the unbiased report. Use rows the search never saw.

feedback.correct: The score that chose the model cannot also report on it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what job the 0.277 has already done.

byKey.best: You reported the best CV score as the expected test score. It is the minimum of 15 estimates, so it flatters the winner.

explain.text: Each cell’s CV score has noise; the minimum of 15 tends to have caught some lucky noise. One evaluation on the locked test set removes that bias. Lesson 4 measures it without a test set, by nested CV.

widget.solution:
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, KFold

def grid_search_best(X_train, y_train, param_grid):
    pipe = Pipeline([('scale', StandardScaler()), ('ridge', Ridge())])
    search = GridSearchCV(pipe, param_grid,
                          cv=KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0),
                          scoring='neg_mean_squared_error')
    search.fit(X_train, y_train)
    return search.best_params_['ridge__alpha']

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_loans(n, p, seed):
    """Loans: spread over base rate (percentage points). x0 leverage +0.6, x1 interest cover -0.4,
    x2 sector risk +0.3, the rest pure noise; noise sd 0.45."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, p)).round(3)
    beta = np.zeros(p)
    beta[:3] = [0.6, -0.4, 0.3][:p]
    y = (2.5 + X @ beta + rng.normal(0, 0.45, n)).round(3)
    return X, y

def make_noise(n, p, seed):
    """Loans whose p signals are all pure noise: spread = 2.5 + noise sd 0.45, unrelated to X."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, p)).round(3)
    y = (2.5 + rng.normal(0, 0.45, n)).round(3)
    return X, y

feedback.correct: Your search agrees with scikit-learn on every grid.

explain.text: The pipeline refits the scaler inside every fold, so no fold sees another’s means. With `refit=True`, the default, the search ends by fitting the best setting on all the training rows. That refitted model is what you score once on the test set.

screens.title: Tune, then test
screens.prose: Put the honest tuning procedure in order.
screens.question: Order the steps from first to last.

lines.text: Split off the test rows and lock them
Run `GridSearchCV` on the training rows only
Read `best_params_`; the search refits that setting on all training rows
Score the refitted model once on the test rows
Report the test score and the grid that was searched

hints.text: What must happen before any data is used to choose?
The test rows are locked first, or at least before the search.
Lock, build, search, refit, score once, report.

feedback.correct: The test rows wait, untouched, until one final score.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The test rows must be locked before the search and used once after it.

explain.text: Locking the test rows first means the search cannot see them. Building the pipeline uses no data, so it may come first too. After the refit the test rows give one score; the report names the grid, showing how much was searched.

screens.title: Choosing a lookback
screens.prose: A momentum signal can look back 5 to 60 days. A researcher picked 20 days by eyeballing backtests of the whole sample. A colleague suggests choosing the lookback by cross-validation on the training years, with later years locked.
screens.question: What does the colleague’s method fix?

options.text: The lookback is chosen on rows it is not judged on, so its score is not inflated by the choice
It guarantees a better lookback than 20 days
options.why: CV may pick 20 days too. What changes is that the reported score no longer contains the choice.

options.text: Nothing: eyeballing and CV both look at data
options.why: Both look, but the eyeballed backtest scores the choice on the very rows that made it. CV keeps choosing and scoring apart.

options.text: It removes the need for a locked test period
options.why: The CV score still did the choosing. The locked years give the clean final number.

hints.text: Which rows judged the 20-day choice?
The eyeballed backtest used every year both to pick and to score.
CV picks on held-out folds of the training years; the locked years then score once.

feedback.correct: Choosing and judging on different rows is the whole point.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which rows the chosen lookback is scored on.

explain.text: Eyeballing a full-sample backtest is tuning on the test set. CV on the training years separates the choice from the score, and the locked years report once. Because returns arrive in time order, the folds must respect time; level 2 shows how.

screens.title: Reading a research note
screens.prose: A spread model's research note says: “$\alpha$ chosen by 5-fold CV on 2015 to 2021; 2022 to 2023 held out. Test MSE 0.23.”
screens.question: Select all that apply.

options.text: The choice of $\alpha$ never saw 2022 to 2023
If 2022 to 2023 was scored once, 0.23 is a fair estimate for loans like those
Random folds within 2015 to 2021 may let later years inform earlier ones; level 2 deals with that
The CV score on 2015 to 2021 is the expected error for 2022 to 2023
options.why: The CV score chose $\alpha$, so it is optimistic, and later years may differ. The held-out years answer that question.

options.text: Refitting on 2015 to 2023 before deployment invalidates the 0.23
options.why: Refitting the frozen recipe on more rows is normal. The 0.23 describes the recipe; the refit usually does slightly better.

hints.text: Which rows did the tuning see?
The held-out years are clean if they were scored once.
Three statements hold; the CV score and the refit claims do not.

feedback.correct: A clean held-out period, with one caution about time order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate what the tuning saw from what was held out.

explain.text: The line is good practice: tuning on earlier years and one score on later ones. The CV number itself is optimistic and is not the forecast. The remaining worry is the random folds inside 2015 to 2021, which level 2 replaces with forward-moving folds.

ideas: Choose a hyperparameter by its cross-validated score on the training rows, never by training error or the test set.
Widen a grid whose best value sits on its edge; within the fold noise, prefer the simpler model.
The best CV score was selected, so it is optimistic. Refit the winner and score it once on the locked test set.

formula.name: One-standard-error rule
formula.note: For ridge, a larger $\alpha$ is a simpler model.

summary.trap: Reporting the best cross-validated score as the expected score on new data.

quiz.prose: Edge case: a grid of one. `GridSearchCV(Ridge(), {'alpha': [30]}, cv=folds)` is run.
quiz.question: How does its `best_score_` compare with `cross_val_score(Ridge(alpha=30), ..., cv=folds)`?

options.text: They are the same number: with one setting nothing is selected, so nothing is flattered
It is lower, because it is the best of the grid
options.why: A best of one is just the one. There is no competition, so no selection bias.

options.text: It is higher, because GridSearchCV refits on all rows
options.why: The refit happens after scoring and does not change `best_score_`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many settings competed.

explain.text: Selection bias comes from picking the minimum of several noisy scores. With one setting, `best_score_` is the plain CV score. The optimism grows with the size of the search.

quiz.prose: Edge case: two settings tie. $\alpha = 0.01$ and $\alpha = 0.03$ both score 0.2025, with the same sd.
quiz.question: Which should you choose?

options.text: $\alpha = 0.03$, the more shrunk model, in the spirit of the one-standard-error rule
$\alpha = 0.01$, because a smaller penalty fits the data better
options.why: It fits the training rows a touch better, but the held-out scores say the two predict equally well. Prefer the simpler.

options.text: Average the two models’ predictions
options.why: Possible, but needless: the two models are nearly identical. A tie is settled by preferring the simpler one.

feedback.correct: When the data cannot separate them, take the simpler model.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. With equal scores, which model is simpler?

explain.text: Equal CV scores mean the data cannot tell the settings apart. More shrinkage means fewer effective parameters, so prefer it. GridSearchCV itself would take the first in the list.

quiz.prose: An analyst tries ten values of $k$ for $k$-nearest neighbours and scores each on the test set. The analyst keeps the best and reports its test MSE.
quiz.question: What has gone wrong?

options.text: The test set did the tuning, so the reported score is the best of ten and biased low
Nothing, as long as the test set is large
options.why: A large test set reduces noise in each score. But the best of ten still flatters the winner, and no clean set is left.

options.text: $k$-nearest neighbours cannot be tuned
options.why: It can, by CV on the training rows.

feedback.correct: Tune on the training rows; test once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which rows chose $k$.

explain.text: Choosing $k$ on the test rows turns them into validation rows. The fix: tune $k$ by CV on the training rows, then score the winner once on the test rows.

quiz.prose: A notebook calls `GridSearchCV(pipe, grid, cv=5)` on a file of loans sorted by size.
quiz.question: What folds does `cv=5` give for this regression?

options.text: `KFold(5)` without shuffling: consecutive blocks of the sorted file
Five shuffled folds
options.why: An integer `cv` builds `KFold(n_splits=5)`, which does not shuffle. Pass `KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)` yourself.

options.text: Stratified folds
options.why: Stratified folds are the default only for classifiers. For a regression an integer gives plain, unshuffled `KFold`.

feedback.correct: On a sorted file that repeats lesson 2’s trap.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what `KFold` does without `shuffle=True`.

explain.text: For a regressor, `cv=5` means `KFold(5)` with no shuffle. On a sorted file each fold is a block of sizes the others never saw. Pass a shuffled `KFold` explicitly.
